idiom_name: one package per directory: exported (capitalized) names, internal/ for module-private code
implementation_notes: Go makes the pattern structural: each directory is exactly one package, imported by path, and the published surface is precisely the exported (capitalized) identifiers - everything lowercase is invisible outside the package. Packages that must not be imported from outside the module go under internal/, a rule the compiler enforces relative to the parent directory tree, and the official layout guide recommends keeping supporting packages there so their API stays free to change. Import cycles are compile errors, so 'low coupling between modules' is not a guideline but a build constraint.
pitfalls: Anything exported is part of the module's API indefinitely: a helper type or field added to the published surface creates a support obligation, so export late and deliberately.
The package name appears in every qualified reference (billing.NewInvoice), so a vague module name such as util, common or model makes every call site vaguer and hides which concept is meant.
Import cycles are rejected outright, which forces a boundary decision at compile time - valuable pressure, but it can require moving a concept or introducing an interface earlier than expected.
The internal/ rule is lexical and parent-relative, so moving a package deeper in the tree can silently widen or narrow who may import it.
